🚨 THE GLOBAL MONETARY SYSTEM IS QUIETLY GOING DIGITAL

Russia and India are reportedly working on a mechanism that would allow digital currencies to be used for bilateral trade payments, according to Sberbank CEO Herman Gref.

Don’t overlook the significance of this.

This isn’t simply another “crypto story.” It is another piece of a much larger transformation occurring across the global financial system.

For decades, international trade has depended heavily on the U.S. dollar, correspondent banks and Western-controlled financial infrastructure.

Now countries are actively building alternatives.

Russia and India are exploring digital-currency settlement for trade.

Iran is increasingly using crypto—including Tether and Bitcoin—to facilitate cross-border commerce under sanctions.

The UK House of Lords just backed an amendment calling for a national digital-assets strategy covering crypto, stablecoins, CBDCs and tokenized securities.

Meanwhile, major financial institutions are rapidly expanding into stablecoins, tokenized assets and blockchain settlement.

This doesn’t mean Bitcoin suddenly replaces the dollar tomorrow.

It means something potentially much bigger is happening:

The infrastructure underneath MONEY itself is changing.

Cash → digital money
Bank ledgers → tokenized assets
Traditional settlement → blockchain/digital settlement
Domestic experiments → international trade

And perhaps the most important part:

Russia and India aren’t talking about digital currencies for speculation.

They’re talking about using them to settle actual international commerce.

That’s the threshold worth watching.

We may be moving from the era where cryptocurrency was considered an alternative financial asset into an era where digital assets and digital currencies become part of the plumbing of the global economy.

The question is no longer simply:

“Will crypto survive?”

The much larger question may be:

“What does the global monetary system look like when virtually everything becomes digital?”

📡 BRICS condemns unilateral tariffs, coercive measures

📌 Tehran, IRNA – The BRICS countries have voiced serious concern over the rise of unilateral tariffs and non-tariff measures that distort trade and violate World Trade Organization rules, while condemning unilateral coercive measures that violate international law.

The New Delhi Declaration, adopted at the 18th BRICS Summit in India on Saturday, emphasized the need for stronger efforts in conflict prevention, particularly by addressing the root causes of conflict, India Today reported.
​
The member nations reaffirmed their commitment to resolving international disputes peacefully through dialogue, consultation, and diplomacy.
​
Additionally, they advocated for a more representative, democratic, and multipolar international order grounded in the UN Charter and international law, calling for greater representation of emerging markets and developing countries.
​
The BRICS countries condemned unilateral economic and secondary sanctions, describing them as contrary to international law and warning that they can harm development, food security, health, and human rights.
​
The declaration also expressed concern over the increasing use of unilateral tariffs, non-tariff barriers, and protectionist measures, which disrupt global trade and supply chains.
​
Regarding global conflicts, the BRICS called for dialogue, diplomacy, preventive diplomacy, and mediation as effective means to resolve international disputes and conflicts.
​
Overall, the New Delhi Declaration emphasized the expanding role of the BRICS grouping in global governance, economic cooperation, and conflict resolution.
